## Statement

Let $x_1<\cdots<x_r$ be natural interpolation knots, $r\ge2$, and put
$h_i=x_{i+1}-x_i$ and $H=\max_i h_i$. Let $s$ be the natural cubic
interpolant with data $y_i$ and nodal second derivatives $M_i$, with
$M_1=M_r=0$. Let $\widehat M_1=\widehat M_r=0$ and let
$\widehat s$ be the piecewise cubic formed from the same values $y_i$ and
the second derivatives $\widehat M_i$ using the natural cubic piece formula
of [[thm-natural-cubic-interpolant-exists-uniquely-at-distinct-knots]]. On
the knot hull $[x_1,x_r]$, if
$$E=\max_{1\le i\le r}|\widehat M_i-M_i|,$$
then
$$\|\widehat s-s\|_{L^\infty([x_1,x_r])}\le \frac{H^2}{8}E.$$

1.1 Fix $i$ and write $h=h_i$ and $t=(x-x_i)/h\in[0,1]$. Subtract the two piece formulas in [F1]. The endpoint values cancel, leaving $\widehat s(x)-s(x)=\frac{h^2}{6}\left((\widehat M_i-M_i)((1-t)^3-(1-t))+(\widehat M_{i+1}-M_{i+1})(t^3-t)\right)$. [given, F1, A1, algebra]

## Definition

For an integer $J\ge0$, put $h=2^{-J}$ and $I_{J,k}=[kh,(k+1)h]$ for $0\le k<2^J$. For an integrable real function $f$ on $[0,1]$, its Haar cell-average projection is the piecewise constant function
$$P_Jf(x)=\frac1h\int_{I_{J,k}}f(t)\,dt\quad\text{when }x\in[kh,(k+1)h).$$
The value at $x=1$ is defined by the average on the last cell. The half-open intervals give an unambiguous partition for point values; changing endpoint values does not change the integrals or the $L^2$ error.

## Definition

For an integer $J\ge3$, a coarse block $a=(a_0,a_1,a_2,a_3)$, a real $s>0$, and $p>0$, define the finite wavelet-coefficient Besov quasi-norm
$$\|(a,d)\|_{b^s_{p,p}(J)}^p=\sum_{\nu=0}^3|a_\nu|^p+\sum_{j=2}^{J-1}2^{jp(s+1/2-1/p)}\sum_{k=0}^{2^j-1}|d_{j,k}|^p.$$
This is the wavelet coefficient convention, with one coarse block and detail blocks indexed by their number $2^j$ of coefficients. At the critical relation $p=(s+1/2)^{-1}$, every scale weight equals $1$, so the quasi-norm is exactly the $\ell^p$ quasi-norm of the full coefficient vector. This finite coefficient definition does not assert equivalence with an intrinsic function-space Besov norm.

## Definition

Let $a<b$, $\omega\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb C$ be continuous, and $g:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Define
$$I_\omega(f,g;[a,b]) := \int_a^b f(x)e^{i\omega g(x)}\,dx.$$
The complex Riemann integral here means the real Riemann integral of the real part plus $i$ times the real Riemann integral of the imaginary part. Euler's formula [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]] and continuity of sine and cosine, which follows from [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]] and differentiability implying continuity [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]], make $e^{i\omega g}$ continuous. The product is continuous, so both component integrals exist by [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]. A function is in $C^r[a,b]$ when it and its derivatives through order $r$ are continuous on $[a,b]$, with one-sided endpoint derivatives. A phase is nonstationary on $[a,b]$ when $g\in C^1[a,b]$ and $|g'(x)|\ge c$ everywhere for some fixed $c>0$. For such a phase and differentiable $h$, put $T_g^0h=h$ and $T_g^{j+1}h=(T_g^jh/g')'$ whenever that derivative exists.

This is an exact-real definition. A later numerical implementation must separately state its moment errors and any floating-point solve error.

## Definition

Let $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$ over $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ with $m,n\ge1$, and let $I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k)$ and $J=(j_1,\ldots,j_k)$ be ordered lists of distinct row and column indices. For $k=0$, both lists and all selected matrices have zero size, with ordinary empty-matrix multiplication. Define $C=A(:,J)\in\mathbb F^{m\times k}$, $R=A(I,:)\in\mathbb F^{k\times n}$, and the cross matrix $W=A(I,J)\in\mathbb F^{k\times k}$, using the same orders in $I,J,W$.

The **skeleton CUR core** is $U_{\mathrm{skel}}=W^\dagger$ and its reconstruction is $\widehat A_{\mathrm{skel}}=C W^\dagger R$. The **projected least-squares CUR core** is $U_{\mathrm{proj}}=C^\dagger A R^\dagger$ and its reconstruction is
$\widehat A_{\mathrm{proj}}=C(C^\dagger A R^\dagger)R=(CC^\dagger)A(R^\dagger R)$.

For $k=0$, both reconstructions are the zero $m\times n$ matrix.

The Moore-Penrose theorem in the dependencies guarantees that these formulas are single-valued for singular as well as nonsingular $C,R,W$. The two core choices are distinct. The projection residual bound on the A page applies only to $\widehat A_{\mathrm{proj}}$; it is not asserted for the skeleton core $W^\dagger$.

## Definition

For real $z>0$, let $D_z:=z^{-1}\frac{d}{dz}$ and define, for integers $\ell\ge0$,
$$j_\ell(z):=(-z)^\ell D_z^\ell\left(\frac{\sin z}{z}\right),\qquad h_\ell^{(1)}(z):=(-z)^\ell D_z^\ell\left(-i\frac{e^{iz}}{z}\right).$$
The definition fixes the outgoing $e^{iz}$ convention. The functions solve the radial Helmholtz equation and have the recurrence, origin, Wronskian, and infinity behavior by [[lem-spherical-bessel-and-hankel-radial-solutions]].

These symbolic definitions assert no stable or certified numerical evaluation algorithm for large $\ell$ or $z$.

## Definition

Let $a<b$ and choose an integer $N\ge1$ and points
$$a=x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_N=b.$$
The **oriented interval mesh** is the ordered family of cells $I_j=(x_{j-1},x_j)$, $1\le j\le N$, each oriented from left to right. Write $h_j=x_j-x_{j-1}>0$. For an integer $p\ge0$, the **broken polynomial space** is
$$V_h^{\mathrm{br}}=\prod_{j=1}^N\mathbb P_p(I_j),$$
with functions interpreted cell by cell. At an interior node $x_j$, write $w^-_j=w|_{I_j}(x_j)$ for the trace from the left cell and $w^+_j=w|_{I_{j+1}}(x_j)$ for the trace from the right cell; the chosen face normal points from left to right, and the jump is $[w]_j=w^+_j-w^-_j$. At $a$ and $b$, the outward normals are $-1$ and $+1$, respectively.

The published matching-affine-simplicial-mesh convention used elsewhere on the A page has dimension $d\ge2$. This definition supplies the distinct one-dimensional interval and trace convention; it makes no assertion about multidimensional cells.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, let $\widehat S_d$ be the reference simplex, and let $F_K(\widehat x)=b+B\widehat x$ map $\overline{\widehat S_d}$ affinely onto a nondegenerate closed simplex $K$, with $\det B>0$. Sobolev spaces on $K$ mean spaces on its open interior. For every scalar $u\in W^{1,2}(K)$ and vector field $G\in W^{1,2}(K;\mathbb R^d)$, each physical facet has bounded $L^2$ traces $\gamma_Fu$ and $\gamma_FG$, obtained by affine transfer from the reference trace maps. These traces are independent of the chosen orientation-preserving reference map, and they satisfy
$$\int_K u\,\operatorname{div}G+\nabla u\cdot G\,dx=\sum_{F\subset\partial K}\int_F(\gamma_Fu)(\gamma_FG)\cdot n_{K,F}\,dS,$$
where $n_{K,F}$ is the outward unit normal.

1.1 Put $\widehat u=u\circ F_K$ and $\widehat G=\det(B)B^{-1}(G\circ F_K)$. By [F2], both belong to $W^{1,2}(\widehat S_d)$. Define the physical traces by $\gamma_Fu(F_K(\widehat x))=\gamma_{\widehat F}\widehat u(\widehat x)$ and $\gamma_FG(F_K(\widehat x))=(\det B)^{-1}B\gamma_{\widehat F}\widehat G(\widehat x)$. The reference traces in [F3] are in $L^2(\widehat F)$; the constant affine surface Jacobian $\det(B)|B^{-T}\widehat n_{\widehat F}|>0$ from [F4] and the fixed matrix factor show these definitions give bounded $L^2(F)$ traces. For a fixed map, [F5] supplies smooth approximants to $\widehat u$ and each component of $G\circ F_K$; the reverse estimate in [F2] maps them to smooth approximants on $K$. Thus smooth functions on $K$ are dense in $W^{1,2}(K)$, and any two bounded affine-transfer trace maps agree on this dense smooth class, so they agree on all of $W^{1,2}(K)$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F8, given]

## Definition

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded Lebesgue-measurable set, let $M:=|D|$, let $q\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb C)$, and let $k\in\mathbb R$. Here $L^2$ and $L^\infty$ are equivalence classes modulo null functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), and $L^\infty$ means essentially bounded with respect to Lebesgue measure ([[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]]). We regard $q$ as zero off $D$. The convention is the volume equation
$$u=f+K_k u,\qquad K_k u(x):=\int_D G_k(x-y)q(y)u(y)\,dy,\qquad G_k(z):=\frac{e^{ik|z|}}{4\pi|z|}\quad(z\ne0).$$
Set $G_k(0):=0$; when $M>0$ the diagonal in $D\times D$ is product-null, so this value is only a representative convention. The input and unknown are classes in complex $L^2(D)$, and the displayed equation is interpreted as an equality of those classes. Its formula is well defined by [[lem-volume-integral-operator-well-defined-and-bounded]].

The associated far-field map is
$$\mathcal F_k[v](\theta):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_D e^{-ik\theta\cdot y}q(y)v(y)\,dy,\qquad \theta\in S^2.$$
Here $S^2$ has the surface measure of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. The map is well defined as a continuous function of $\theta$ by [[lem-volume-far-field-map-is-bounded]].

For $x\notin\overline D$, the exterior volume potential is
$$V_kv(x):=\int_D G_k(x-y)q(y)v(y)\,dy.$$
This is absolutely convergent because $x$ has positive distance from the compact set $\overline D$ and $qv\in L^1(D)$.

If $M=0$, define $L^2(D)=\{0\}$ and $K_k=0$; all solution and far-field statements on that space are the zero-space statements. The substantive operator results below assume $0<M<\infty$.

This is a stipulated integral-equation model with the sign convention $(-\Delta-k^2)(u-f)=q u$ when the corresponding distributional Helmholtz equation is used. In the acoustic notation of Scherzer–Mindrinos, their equation $u=u_i-k^2\Phi*((1-n)u)$ corresponds to $q=k^2(n-1)$. No existence or uniqueness for all contrasts is asserted by this definition.

## Definition

$$u=f+K_k u,\qquad K_k u(x):=\int_D G_k(x-y)q(y)u(y)\,dy,\qquad G_k(z):=\frac{e^{ik|z|}}{4\pi|z|}\quad(z\ne0).$$
Set $G_k(0):=0$; when $M>0$ the diagonal in $D\times D$ is product-null, so this value is only a representative convention. The input and unknown are classes in complex $L^2(D)$, and the displayed equation is interpreted as an equality of those classes. Its formula is well defined by [[lem-volume-integral-operator-well-defined-and-bounded]].

The associated far-field map is
$$\mathcal F_k[v](\theta):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_D e^{-ik\theta\cdot y}q(y)v(y)\,dy,\qquad \theta\in S^2.$$
Here $S^2$ has the surface measure of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. The map is well defined as a continuous function of $\theta$ by [[lem-volume-far-field-map-is-bounded]].

## Definition

Let $d\ge1$ and $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ have a finite cell partition $\mathcal T$. Let $V_h$ be a finite-dimensional vector space of continuous vector-valued functions, each cellwise polynomial, and let $Q_h$ be a finite-dimensional scalar space of continuous cellwise polynomials with zero mean. Boundary conditions are stated with each application; the Stokes theorem below uses zero velocity boundary values, and the periodic example below uses periodic identification. The pair is **equal order** when velocity components and pressure use the same polynomial degree on each cell. On a cell $K$, derivatives in residuals are classical derivatives restricted to the cell interior. For well-defined cell integrals, take $\sigma\in L^\infty(\Omega)$, $ eta\in L^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^d)$, $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^d)$, and parameters $	au_K\ge0$, $\gamma\ge0$.

For viscosity $
u>0$, reaction coefficient $\sigma\ge0$, advective field $ eta$, force $f$, and trial pair $(u_h,p_h)\in V_h	imes Q_h$, define the strong momentum residual
$$R_{M,K}(u_h,p_h):=\sigma u_h+ eta\cdot
abla u_h-
u\Delta_Ku_h+
abla p_h-f.$$
For test pairs $(v_h,q_h)$, the full residual PSPG mixed form is
$$B_h((u_h,p_h),(v_h,q_h)):=
u(
abla u_h,
abla v_h)_\Omega+( eta\cdot
abla u_h+\sigma u_h,v_h)_\Omega-(p_h,
abla\cdot v_h)_\Omega+(q_h,
abla\cdot u_h)_\Omega+\sum_K	au_K(
abla q_h,\sigma u_h+ eta\cdot
abla u_h-
u\Delta_Ku_h+
abla p_h)_K,$$
with load $(f,v_h)_\Omega+\sum_K	au_K(
abla q_h,f)_K$. The **grad-div** addend in velocity tests $v_h$ is $\gamma\sum_K(
abla\cdot u_h,
abla\cdot v_h)_K$ with $\gamma\ge0$. This definition alone asserts no inf-sup condition, pressure bound, energy estimate, or convergence result.

For piecewise affine velocities, $\Delta_Ku_h=0$ on each cell. Therefore the standard P1 PSPG residual omits the cellwise viscous Laplacian of the exact velocity; this fact does not justify a pressure-accuracy or convergence claim. Such conclusions require separate consistency and stabilization analysis.

## Statement

Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, $\ell_j>0$, and let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval containing $[0,T]$. Suppose $b:J\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ is $C^1$ and periodic in $x_j$ with period $\ell_j$ for every $j$. Choose a compact interval $K\subset J$ with $[0,T]\subset\operatorname{int}K$, and put $M_K:=\sup_{K\times[0,\ell_1]\times\cdots\times[0,\ell_d]}\|b\|_2$. For every $s\in[0,T]$ and $x\in\mathbb R^d$, there is a unique solution $X(\cdot;s,x)$ of
$$X'(t)=b(t,X(t)),\qquad X(s;s,x)=x,$$
on the whole interval $[0,T]$. The lifted flow is periodic-equivariant:
$$X(t;s,x+\boldsymbol k\boldsymbol\ell)=X(t;s,x)+\boldsymbol k\boldsymbol\ell\qquad(\boldsymbol k\in\mathbb Z^d),$$
where $\boldsymbol k\boldsymbol\ell=(k_1\ell_1,\ldots,k_d\ell_d)$. If $M_T:=\sup_{[0,T]\times[0,\ell_1]\times\cdots\times[0,\ell_d]}\|b\|_2$, then
$$\|X(t;s,x)-x\|_2\le M_T|t-s|\qquad(t\in[0,T]).$$
Thus each characteristic stays in a compact tube $[0,T]\times\overline B(x,M_TT+1)$.

1.1 Periodicity and continuity on the compact cylinder $K\times[0,\ell_1]\times\cdots\times[0,\ell_d]$ give finite bounds $M_K:=\sup\|b\|_2$ and $L:=\sup\|D_xb\|$ there. The same bounds hold on all spatial translates. By [F5] each time slice is globally $L$-Lipschitz in $x$. Since $[0,T]\subset\operatorname{int}K$, choose $\delta>0$ small enough that every radius-$\delta$ time interval centered in $[0,T]$ lies in $K$, $\delta(M_K+1)\le1$, and $\delta(L+1)<1$. On each corresponding unit-radius state cylinder, [F2] therefore gives a unique local solution through its center. [given, F2, F5, choose]

## Statement

Let $x_1<\cdots<x_r$, $r\ge3$, and let $s$ be the natural cubic
interpolant of nodal values $y_i$. Write $h_i=x_{i+1}-x_i$ and
$H=\max_i h_i$. Let $A$ be the $(r-2)\times(r-2)$ interior coefficient
matrix in the system of
[[thm-natural-cubic-interpolant-exists-uniquely-at-distinct-knots]], and
let $b$ be its right-hand side. Put
$$\delta=\min_{2\le i\le r-1}(h_{i-1}+h_i)>0.$$
For any proposed nodal second derivatives
$\widehat M_1=\widehat M_r=0$, let $\widehat m$ be their interior vector,
let $\rho=A\widehat m-b$ be the exact residual, and let $\widehat s$ be
the piecewise cubic given by the natural piece formula with these second
derivatives and the same values $y_i$. Then, on the knot hull,
$$\|\widehat s-s\|_{L^\infty([x_1,x_r])}\le \frac{H^2}{8\delta}\|\rho\|_\infty.$$
This is a residual-to-function transfer statement; it does not assert that
a particular floating-point solver returns a residual certificate.

1.1 Let $e=\widehat m-m$, so $Ae=\rho$ by [F1] and the definition of $\rho$. Choose an index $i$ at which $|e_i|=\|e\|_\infty$, and put $S_i=h_{i-1}+h_i$. The diagonal entry in row $i$ is $2S_i$, while the sum $R_i$ of the absolute off-diagonal entries is at most $S_i$ because an endpoint row omits the coefficient multiplying the fixed zero endpoint second derivative (and when $r=3$ there are no off-diagonal entries). The reverse triangle inequality and $|e_j|\le\|e\|_\infty$ give $|\rho_i|\ge(2S_i-R_i)\|e\|_\infty\ge S_i\|e\|_\infty\ge\delta\|e\|_\infty$. Hence $\|e\|_\infty\le\|\rho\|_\infty/\delta$. selected floating-point system. Compute its Leibniz determinant by forming each

second kind.

## Statement

Let $p>0$ and $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^3$. If any component of $\alpha$ is odd, then
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}x^\alpha e^{-p\|x\|_2^2}\,dx=0.$$
If $\alpha_j=2k_j$ for $j=1,2,3$, then
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}x^\alpha e^{-p\|x\|_2^2}\,dx=\pi^{3/2}\prod_{j=1}^3\frac{(2k_j)!}{4^{k_j}k_j!\,p^{k_j+1/2}}.$$
For every $q\in\mathbb N_0$, differentiation with respect to $p$ is valid and
$$\frac{d^q}{dp^q}\int_{\mathbb R^3}x^\alpha e^{-p\|x\|_2^2}\,dx=(-1)^q\int_{\mathbb R^3}\|x\|_2^{2q}x^\alpha e^{-p\|x\|_2^2}\,dx.$$

1.1 In one dimension, scaling $y=\sqrt p\,x$ and [F1], [F7] give $J_0(p):=\int e^{-px^2}dx=\sqrt\pi\,p^{-1/2}$. Odd moments vanish by the substitution $x\mapsto-x$. For $k\ge1$, integration by parts [F2] on $[-R,R]$ with $dv=xe^{-px^2}dx=-d(e^{-px^2})/(2p)$ gives $J_k(p)=(2k-1)J_{k-1}(p)/(2p)$ after $R\to\infty$; the boundary term is a polynomial times $e^{-pR^2}$ and tends to zero. Iterating yields $J_k(p)=\sqrt\pi(2k)!/(4^k k!p^{k+1/2})$. [given, F1, F2, F7, algebra]

[[def-conservative-finite-volume-scheme]]. For $J_n^m=[t_n^m,t_{n+1}^m)$,

$$ \mathcal U_m(x,t)=U_j^{m,n},\qquad \mathcal Q_m(x,t)=Q_{j+1/2}^{m,n} $$ whenever $(x,t)\in I_j^m\times J_n^m$. ## Definition

For Burgers' flux $f_B(s)=s^2/2$, define $G\colon\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ as follows. If $a\le b$, set
$$ G(a,b)=\begin{cases} a^2/2,&a\ge0,\\ b^2/2,&a<0\text{ and }b\le0,\\ 0,&a<0<b. \end{cases} $$ If $b<a$, set $$ G(a,b)=\frac12\max\{a^2,b^2\}. $$
This is the Godunov flux for the convex Burgers flux: for increasing states it
uses the minimum of $f_B$ on $[a,b]$, and for decreasing states it uses the
maximum of $f_B$ on $[b,a]$. It is proposed as a particular numerical flux in
the scheme of [[def-conservative-finite-volume-scheme]]. Its continuity and
consistency are verified in the pair.

## Statement

Let $u\in C^2$ on a neighborhood of a cell and its two neighbors, and suppose $|u'(x)|\ge c>0$ there. Let $U_j$ be the averages of $u$ over uniform cells of width $h$, centered at $x_j=x_0+jh$. For sufficiently small $h$, the MUSCL/minmod face states of [[def-na-high-resolution-reconstruction]] satisfy
$$|U_i+hs_i/2-u(x_i+h/2)|\le C h^2,\qquad |U_i-hs_i/2-u(x_i-h/2)|\le C h^2,$$
where $C$ depends only on $c$ and a bound for $|u''|$ on the stated neighborhood.

2.1 Because $|u'(x_i)|\ge c$, both increments in step 1.1 have the same nonzero sign for all sufficiently small $h$. Minmod selects one of them, and either equals $hu'(x_i)+O(M_2h^2)$; hence $hs_i=hu'(x_i)+O(M_2h^2)$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

## Example

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\mu$ be Lebesgue measure on $[0,1]$, take $\alpha=1/4$, $\beta=1/2$,
and set $k(x,y)=\alpha+\beta xy$ and $f(x)=1$. The equation
$$u(x)-\int_{[0,1]}k(x,y)u(y)\,d\mu(y)=1$$
has the unique solution
$$u(x)=\frac{80+24x}{57}.$$
The two-node Gaussian rule for $\mu$ gives the exact same solution and a
nonsingular two-by-two grid system. The continuous integrals can equivalently
be read as Riemann integrals under Countable Choice.

3.1 Any solution $v$ of the inhomogeneous two-node Nyström equation has the form $v(x)=1+\alpha Q_2(v)+\beta xQ_2(yv)$, hence is affine. Exactness [F3] then makes its two moments satisfy the same nonsingular system in step 1.1, so those moments and the reconstructed function are unique; step 2.1 supplies existence. A nonzero vector in the grid-matrix kernel would, by the nullspace correspondence [F5], give a nonzero homogeneous solution, which could be added to this solution and contradict uniqueness. Thus the grid matrix is nonsingular, and its reconstruction is the displayed solution. [F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a shape-regular affine $d$-simplex,
$F\subset\partial K$ a facet, and $1/2<r\le1$. Every $q\in H^r(K)$ has a
single-valued $L^2(F)$ trace $\gamma_Fq$. For $1/2<r<1$,
$$\|\gamma_Fq\|_{L^2(F)} \le C\left(h_K^{-1/2}\|q\|_{L^2(K)} +h_K^{r-1/2}[q]_{H^r(K)}\right),$$
and
$$\|\gamma_Fq-\operatorname{avg}_F\gamma_Fq\|_{L^2(F)} \le C h_K^{r-1/2}[q]_{H^r(K)},$$
while for $r=1$,
$$\|\gamma_Fq\|_{L^2(F)} \le C\left(h_K^{-1/2}\|q\|_{L^2(K)} +h_K^{1/2}\|\nabla q\|_{L^2(K)}\right),$$
and the face-mean fluctuation is bounded by
$C h_K^{1/2}\|\nabla q\|_{L^2(K)}$.
The constant depends only on $d$, the shape-regularity bound, and $r$.

If $u\in H^1(K)$, $\nabla u\in H^r(K;\mathbb R^d)$, and
$f=-\Delta u\in L^2(K)$ distributionally, then for every $w\in H^1(K)$,
$$\int_Kfw\,dx=\int_K\nabla u\cdot\nabla w\,dx -\sum_{F\subset\partial K}\int_F(\gamma_F\nabla u\cdot n_{K,F})\gamma_Fw\,dS.$$
Here $n_{K,F}$ is the outward unit normal. The trace threshold $r>1/2$ is
used to make the normal-gradient trace an $L^2$ function.

The two cell traces of a global $H^1(\Omega)$ function agree on a shared
interior facet, and the trace of a global $H^1_0(\Omega)$ function vanishes
on a boundary facet. More generally, if $1/2<r<1$ and $q\in H^r(\Omega)$,
then its two traces on each shared interior facet agree almost everywhere.

1.2 Fractional extension from the reference simplex. Cover its closed simplex by finitely many affine coordinate neighborhoods: at a point on a face of codimension $m$, the $m$ vanishing barycentric coordinates are independent and the simplex is locally the orthant where those coordinates are positive. Compactness gives a finite cover with smaller compact subsets still covering the closed simplex. By [F5], choose smooth cutoffs supported in the corresponding neighborhoods and equal to one on those smaller sets; divide them by their positive sum near the closed simplex to obtain a finite smooth partition of unity. Multiplication by a smooth cutoff is bounded on $W^{r,2}$: split $\eta(x)q(x)-\eta(y)q(y)$ into $\eta(x)(q(x)-q(y))$ and $(\eta(x)-\eta(y))q(y)$, use $|\eta(x)-\eta(y)|\le\min(\|D\eta\|_\infty|x-y|,2\|\eta\|_\infty)$, and integrate the latter radial kernel, finite exactly for $0<r<1$. Cover its closed simplex by finitely many affine coordinate neighborhoods: at a point on a face of codimension $m$, the $m$ vanishing barycentric coordinates are independent and the simplex is locally the orthant where those coordinates are positive. Compactness gives a finite cover with smaller compact subsets still covering the closed simplex. By [F5], choose smooth cutoffs supported in the corresponding neighborhoods and equal to one on those smaller sets; divide them by their positive sum near the closed simplex to obtain a finite smooth partition of unity. Multiplication by a smooth cutoff is bounded on $W^{r,2}$: split $\eta(x)q(x)-\eta(y)q(y)$ into $\eta(x)(q(x)-q(y))$ and $(\eta(x)-\eta(y))q(y)$, use $|\eta(x)-\eta(y)|\le\min(\|D\eta\|_\infty|x-y|,2\|\eta\|_\infty)$, and integrate the latter radial kernel, finite exactly for $0<r<1$. Each localized piece is supported away from the artificial edge of its chart, so extending by zero there adds at most $C\|q\|_{L^2}^2$ to the seminorm: all cross-pairs have distance at least the support-to-edge distance. In orthant coordinates extend across each active coordinate hyperplane by even reflection. Same-side pairs reproduce the original integral; for opposite-side pairs $(x',t),(y',-s)$ with $t,s>0$, $|(x'-y',t+s)|\ge|(x'-y',t-s)|$, so their Gagliardo integrand is bounded by the corresponding original-side integrand. Iterating over the finitely many active coordinates, pulling back the nonsingular affine charts, and summing the finitely many extensions gives a bounded linear extension $E:W^{r,2}(\widehat S_d)\to W^{r,2}(\mathbb R^d)$. The same construction for $r=1$ uses the ordinary even-reflection weak derivative formula; the zero extension of each compactly supported $W^{1,2}$ localized piece is justified by [F16]. ## Definition

Input: a finite labeled conforming mesh $\mathcal T$, exact nonnegative arrays $(\eta_K^2)_{K\in\mathcal T}$ and $(o_K^2)_{K\in\mathcal T}$, where $\eta_K^2$ is the cell estimator contribution and $o_K^2$ the cell data-oscillation contribution, bulk-fraction parameters $\theta_E,\theta_O\in(0,1]$, a per-call total bisection budget $B\in\mathbb N_0$, and a stable total order of mesh identifiers. For an array $q_K\ge0$ and $\theta\in(0,1]$, sort by decreasing $q_K$ and then increasing identifier. If $\sum_Kq_K=0$, return the empty set. Otherwise return the shortest initial segment whose sum is at least $\theta\sum_Kq_K$. Thus these parameters are fractions of the squared contributions (the square-root convention for the usual estimator-norm parameter). Call the resulting sets $M_E,M_O$ and set $M=M_E\cup M_O$.

Set a remaining-generation flag $q_K=3$ on each cell in $M$ and $q_K=0$ on every other cell. Repeatedly take the pending leaf with least stable identifier and process its reference edge. If the reference edge is on the polygon boundary, bisect that leaf. If its interior reference neighbor has the same generation, bisect the compatible pair simultaneously. If the neighbor has generation one lower, recursively process that neighbor first and then re-inspect the original leaf; this follows the finite reference-edge chain until the edge can be split conformingly. Every split leaf $T$ is replaced by its two children, each inheriting $q_T-1$ when $q_T>0$ and otherwise $0$. Thus conformity splits may propagate without scheduling extra uniform generations, while a marked cell and its descendants complete all three requested generations. Process simultaneous pairs in the same transaction and use the fixed identifier order for all pending leaves. Stop when all remaining-generation flags vanish. Count every bisection against $B$. If closure or a pending request would exceed the remaining budget, discard the tentative forest and return the original mesh with status budget-exhausted; otherwise return the refined matching mesh with status complete. Invalid arrays, nonfinite or negative entries, invalid parameters, or incompatible labels return invalid-input without changing the mesh. ## Definition

Use the uniform mesh, coefficients, and spaces of [[def-supg-one-dimensional-convection-diffusion-model]]. On every cell set
$$\tau=\frac{h}{2|b|}\left(\coth(\mathrm{Pe})-\frac1{\mathrm{Pe}}\right),\qquad \coth s:=\frac{\cosh s}{\sinh s}.$$
For $w\in S_h(g_0,g_1)+C^2([0,1])$ and $v_h\in V_h$, define
$$a_h(w,v_h):=\epsilon\int_0^1w'v_h'\,dx+b\int_0^1w'v_h\,dx+\sum_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\tau\int_K(-\epsilon w''+bw')(bv_h')\,dx,$$
$$F_h(v_h):=\int_0^1fv_h\,dx+\sum_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\tau\int_K f(bv_h')\,dx.$$
Second derivatives are taken classically on each cell. The strong equation residual is $R_K(w):=-\epsilon w''+bw'-f$. For P1 trial functions, $w_h''=0$ on each cell, so the cell term is $\tau\int_K(bw_h')(bv_h')$. On the smooth consistency extension it retains $-\epsilon w''$; thus the full residual pairing is $\tau\int_K(R_K(w)+f)(bv_h')$, while the load contains the matching $f$ term. The SUPG equation is $a_h(w_h,v_h)=F_h(v_h)$ and adds the same residual-weighted streamline test perturbation to the differential equation and its load.

## Statement

Use the block operators and residual closure of [[def-supg-variational-multiscale-block-closure]]. Equip $X_c,X_f$ and their duals with norms, and use the corresponding induced operator norms. Let $G:=A_{ff}^{-1}$, assume the exact Schur system has a solution $u_c$, and put $r_f:=F_f-A_{fc}u_c$. Suppose the closure map $T$ has $\widetilde S:=A_{cc}-A_{cf}TA_{fc}$ invertible, and let $\widetilde u_c$ solve the approximate Schur system. Then
$$\|\widetilde u_c-u_c\|\le\|\widetilde S^{-1}\|\,\|A_{cf}\|\,\|T-G\|\,\|r_f\|,$$
and for the modeled fine component $\widetilde u_f=T(F_f-A_{fc}\widetilde u_c)$,
$$\|\widetilde u_f-u_f\|\le\|T-G\|\,\|r_f\|+\|T\|\,\|A_{fc}\|\,\|\widetilde u_c-u_c\|.$$
The exact fine scale is $u_f=G r_f$. These bounds concern finite-dimensional algebraic blocks; they do not certify a universal PDE subgrid model.

## Definition

For coefficient $a$, cell $Y$, and zero-mean periodic space $V_\#$ from [[def-periodic-scalar-diffusion-data]] and [[def-periodic-zero-mean-cell-space]], and for $p\in\mathbb R^d$, the **weak periodic cell equation** asks for $\chi_p\in V_\#$ such that
$$\int_Y a(y)(p+\nabla_y\chi_p(y))\cdot\nabla_yv(y)\,dy=0\qquad(v\in V_\#).$$
The sign convention is $p+\nabla_y\chi_p$; the zero-mean condition fixes the additive constant. This definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness.

## Definition

Input $a<b$, $\omega\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, real $g\in C^1[a,b]$ with $|g'|\ge c>0$, complex $f\in C[a,b]$, an integer $n\ge2$, linearly independent basis functions $\psi_1,\ldots,\psi_n\in C^1[a,b]$, and distinct collocation nodes $a=x_1<\cdots<x_n=b$. Define $L_\omega\psi=\psi'+i\omega g'\psi$, form $A_{jk}=L_\omega\psi_k(x_j)$ and $y_j=f(x_j)$. If $A$ is singular, return failure status and no quadrature value. Otherwise solve $Ac=y$ in exact arithmetic, put $p=\sum_{k=1}^nc_k\psi_k$, and return
$$Q_L=p(b)e^{i\omega g(b)}-p(a)e^{i\omega g(a)}$$
with $A,c$, and $\kappa_2(A)=\|A\|_2\|A^{-1}\|_2$, where vector norms are Euclidean and $\|A\|_2=\sup_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Av\|_2$ is the induced matrix norm. This is a finite collocation procedure; residual and conditioning claims for the nonsingular branch are stated separately on this page. Rounded factorization error is outside this exact-arithmetic definition.

## Definition

Inputs are those of [[def-spherical-bessel-evaluation-contract]], a nonempty finite list of valid targets, finite exact positive rational absolute tolerances, optional exact positive rational relative tolerances, and finite integer caps $W,Q,M_{\max},p_{\max}\ge1$. $W$ is the maximum exact-arithmetic work count, $Q$ the maximum stage and represented-point interface index, $M_{\max}$ the maximum Taylor degree, and $p_{\max}$ the maximum final dyadic precision. A Gaussian rational is $a+ib$ with $a,b\in\mathbb Q$. A Laurent polynomial is a finite sum $\sum_k a_k z^k$ with integer exponents and Gaussian-rational coefficients; its formal derivative uses $(z^k)'=kz^{k-1}$. An expression graph below is a finite directed acyclic graph of exact rational arithmetic operations.

Factorials are those of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]; they are nonzero by that definition and [[lem-of-naturals-positive]], so every displayed factorial denominator is defined. For a rational $x$, $\lceil x\rceil$ denotes the least integer greater than or equal to $x$, computed by exact integer division.

Reject an invalid order, target, tolerance, cap, or interval input not contained in $(0,\infty)$ with `domain`. For a represented point, an interval returned by the input interface may meet zero; such a stage is skipped and a later interface index is tried.

Construct Laurent polynomials by
$$A_0=0,\quad B_0=z^{-1},\quad C_0=-iz^{-1},$$
$$A_{r+1}=rz^{-1}A_r-A_r'-B_r,\quad B_{r+1}=rz^{-1}B_r-B_r'+A_r,\quad C_{r+1}=rz^{-1}C_r-C_r'-iC_r$$
for $r=0,\ldots,\ell-1$. With $s$ and $c$ denoting the sine and cosine input enclosures, form the unscaled outputs
$$u=A_\ell c+B_\ell s,\quad v=(A_\ell'+B_\ell)c+(B_\ell'-A_\ell)s,\quad w=C_\ell(c+is),\quad t=(C_\ell'+iC_\ell)(c+is).$$
Form the scaled outputs
$$c_\ell z^{-\ell}u,\quad c_\ell z^{-\ell}v,\quad d_\ell^{-1}z^{\ell+1}C_\ell,\quad d_\ell^{-1}z^{\ell+1}(C_\ell'+iC_\ell).$$
Collect like Laurent powers exactly; in particular cancel negative powers in the scaled $h_\ell^{(1)}$ value when they cancel algebraically. A remaining $z^{-1}$ in the scaled derivative is evaluated only on positive input intervals.

For real intervals use exact rational endpoint hulls: $[a,b]+[c,d]=[a+c,b+d]$, $[a,b][c,d]=[\min(ac,ad,bc,bd),\max(ac,ad,bc,bd)]$, and $[a,b]^{-1}=[1/b,1/a]$ when $0<a\le b$. For complex rectangles, apply these real interval operations to the real and imaginary components of $(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$. Thus interval arithmetic encloses every pointwise sum and product; division is only by a positive power of the positive argument or by a positive integer constant. Compute powers, factorials, and rational endpoints by finite exact arithmetic.

At a positive current box $I=[a,b]$, choose $M\ge0$ with $M+2\ge2b$ and form the rational interval polynomial and rational tail
$$T_M(I)=\sum_{m=0}^{M}\frac{(iI)^m}{m!},\qquad E_M=\frac{2b^{M+1}}{(M+1)!}.$$
The interval power is repeated complex-rectangle multiplication. Enclose $\cos(I)$ by $\operatorname{Re}T_M(I)+[-E_M,E_M]$ and $\sin(I)$ by $\operatorname{Im}T_M(I)+[-E_M,E_M]$. Evaluate each requested output graph with these leaves and $z\in I$, and round each final endpoint outward to the grid $2^{-p}\mathbb Z$.

Use the following deterministic finite search. Charge the Laurent recurrence, graph construction, and coefficient collection to the work counter as they are performed. For stages $q=1,\ldots,Q$, first take the fixed interval unchanged, or call the represented-point interface at index $q$. Skip a represented-point stage unless its returned interval has $a>0$. Set $p=q$ and $M=\max(q,\lceil2b\rceil)$. If $p>p_{\max}$ or $M>M_{\max}$, stop with `inconclusive`. Evaluate all requested graphs and the displayed $T_M,E_M$ using the work counter: each exact rational or Gaussian-rational arithmetic operation or comparison, each Taylor term, each endpoint-rounding operation, and each interface call costs one unit. If the next operation would exceed $W$, stop with `inconclusive` before performing it. If the output format cannot represent a certified endpoint, return `range` with no finite claim. If every requested target has radius at most its absolute tolerance, return `success`; for each optional relative tolerance, set its flag true exactly when the enclosure excludes zero and the relative test in the contract passes. A failed relative test does not prevent absolute `success`. If no stage succeeds before a cap or the search ends, return `inconclusive`. No floating-point recurrence is used.

## Statement

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded Lipschitz polyhedron admitting a finite matching affine tetrahedral mesh as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. Use the product spaces $H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):=(H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R))^3$ and $H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):=(H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R))^3$, with $\|v\|_{H^1}^2:=\sum_{j=1}^3(\|v_j\|_2^2+\sum_{|\alpha|=1}\|D^\alpha v_j\|_2^2)$, using the scalar conventions of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]] and [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]. Put $T(\partial\Omega):=H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)/H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with quotient norm $\|[v]\|_T:=\inf_{z\in H_0^1}\|v+z\|_{H^1}$, and write $T(\partial\Omega)'$ for its real norm dual. For $u\in H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$, the formula
$$\langle\gamma_\tau u,[v]\rangle:=\int_\Omega(\operatorname{curl}u\cdot v-u\cdot\operatorname{curl}v)\,dx$$
defines a bounded linear functional on $T(\partial\Omega)$, independent of the representative $v$. For smooth $u$ and smooth $v$ it equals $\int_{\partial\Omega}(n\times u)\cdot v\,dS$. Thus $\gamma_\tau u$ is the weak tangential trace in the trace-quotient norm. In particular, every element of [[def-na-zero-tangential-hcurl]] has zero weak tangential trace. No converse characterization of that closure is asserted here.

1.1 If $v_1-v_2\in H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, choose $\varphi_m\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ converging to $v_1-v_2$ in $H^1$ by [F2]. The difference of the two proposed pairings is $\int_\Omega(\operatorname{curl}u\cdot(v_1-v_2)-u\cdot\operatorname{curl}(v_1-v_2))$. The $L^2$ convergence of both fields and curls permits passage to the limit from $\varphi_m$, and each approximating pairing is zero by [F1]. Hence the formula is independent of the representative. [A1, F1, F2, given, construct]

## Statement

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded Lipschitz polyhedron admitting a finite matching affine tetrahedral mesh as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. Use the product spaces $H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):=(H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R))^3$ and $H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):=(H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R))^3$, with $\|v\|_{H^1}^2:=\sum_{j=1}^3(\|v_j\|_2^2+\sum_{|\alpha|=1}\|D^\alpha v_j\|_2^2)$, using the scalar conventions of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]] and [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]. Put $T(\partial\Omega):=H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)/H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with quotient norm $\|[v]\|_T:=\inf_{z\in H_0^1}\|v+z\|_{H^1}$, and write $T(\partial\Omega)'$ for its real norm dual. For $u\in H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$, the formula
$$\langle\gamma_\tau u,[v]\rangle:=\int_\Omega(\operatorname{curl}u\cdot v-u\cdot\operatorname{curl}v)\,dx$$
defines a bounded linear functional on $T(\partial\Omega)$, independent of the representative $v$. For smooth $u$ and smooth $v$ it equals $\int_{\partial\Omega}(n\times u)\cdot v\,dS$. Thus $\gamma_\tau u$ is the weak tangential trace in the trace-quotient norm. In particular, every element of [[def-na-zero-tangential-hcurl]] has zero weak tangential trace. No converse characterization of that closure is asserted here.

3.1 If $u_m\in C_c^\infty$ converges to $u\in H_0(\operatorname{curl})$ in the graph norm, choose a cutoff $\chi$ equal to one near the compact support of $u_m$ by [F6]. For any $v\in H^1$, $\chi v$ has compact support in $\Omega$ and its zero extension lies in $H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ by [F7]. Choose another cutoff $\theta\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ equal to one on that support. Approximate the zero extension by $g_j\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ using [F7]; then $q_j:=\theta g_j\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ and $q_j\to\chi v$ in $H^1$ by [F8], proving $\chi v\in H_0^1$. For each $j$, [F1] applied to $u_m$ and the compactly supported smooth test $q_j$ gives $\int_\Omega\operatorname{curl}u_m\cdot q_j=\int_\Omega u_m\cdot\operatorname{curl}q_j$. Since $H^1$ convergence implies $L^2$ convergence of both $q_j$ and $\operatorname{curl}q_j$, Cauchy–Schwarz passes this identity to the limit $q_j\to\chi v$. Because $\chi=1$ and $\nabla\chi=0$ on the support of $u_m$, the limiting identity is $\int_\Omega(\operatorname{curl}u_m\cdot v-u_m\cdot\operatorname{curl}v)=0$. Step 2.1 gives $\gamma_\tau u_m\to\gamma_\tau u$ in $T'$, so the limit trace is zero. [A1, F1, F3, F6, F7, F8, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice.

Let $(V,H,J)$ be the evolution triple of
[[def-pe12-gelfand-triple]], $1<p<\infty$, and assume
$A:V\to V^*$ is strongly monotone with constant $\mu>0$ and exponent $p$:
$$\langle A(x)-A(y),x-y\rangle\ge\mu\|x-y\|_V^p \qquad(x,y\in V).$$
Suppose $u,v\in L^p(0,T;V)$ have derivatives in
$L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$ and residual difference
$R=(u'+A(u))-(v'+A(v))\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$. Then for every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$\|u(t)-v(t)\|_H^2+ \mu\int_0^t\|u-v\|_V^p \le\|u(0)-v(0)\|_H^2+ 2C_{\mu,p}\|R\|_{L^{p'}(0,t;V^*)}^{p'},$$
where both functions use their continuous $H$ representatives and
$C_{\mu,p}=\frac1{p'}(2/(\mu p))^{1/(p-1)}$. In particular, equal initial data
and zero residual imply $u=v$.

1.1 Set $e=u-v$. Subtracting the residual definitions gives $e'+A(u)-A(v)=R$ in $L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$. By [F1], testing this identity against $e\in L^p(0,T;V)$ is integrable by [F2], and for every $t$, $$\frac12\|e(t)\|_H^2-\frac12\|e(0)\|_H^2 +\int_0^t\langle A(u)-A(v),e\rangle =\int_0^t\langle R,e\rangle.$$ [A1, A2, F1, F2, given, algebra]

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let a finite metric graph
with nonempty edge set have every connected edge component anchored, let
$V=V_D$ and $H=\bigoplus_{e\in E}L^2(0,\ell_e;\mathbb R)$, and let $V_h$
be its conforming P1 edge space. Put $L_\Gamma=\sum_e\ell_e$,
$\alpha=\kappa_{\min}/(1+L_\Gamma^2)$, and assume constant diffusivities
$0<\kappa_{\min}\le\kappa_e\le\kappa_{\max}$. For $T>0$,
$f\in L^2(0,T;V_D^*)$, and $u_h^0\in V_h$, define
$a(w,v)=\sum_e\kappa_e\int_0^{\ell_e}w'_ev'_e\,dx_e$. There is a unique
$u_h\in H^1(0,T;V_h)$ with $u_h(0)=u_h^0$ satisfying, for almost every $t$,

$$((u_h)'(t),v_h)_H+a(u_h(t),v_h)=\langle f(t),v_h\rangle_{V_D^*,V_D}\qquad(v_h\in V_h).$$

For every $t\in[0,T]$,

$$\|u_h(t)\|_H^2+\alpha\int_0^t\|u_h(s)\|_{V_D}^2\,ds\le\|u_h^0\|_H^2+\alpha^{-1}\int_0^t\|f(s)\|_{V_D^*}^2\,ds.$$

Here $V_h$ is the finite P1 space from
[[def-metric-graph-p1-edge-mesh]]. This is a semidiscrete
existence and energy statement; it gives no parabolic spatial error rate.

1.1 The canonical inclusion $i:V_D\to H$ is continuous because $\|v\|_H\le\|v\|_{V_D}$. It is injective because $V_D$ consists of Sobolev classes included in the edge-product $L^2$ classes. To prove density, fix $g=(g_e)\in H$ and $\epsilon>0$. By [F2] and finite choice, choose for each of the finitely many edges a $\phi_e\in C_c^\infty(0,\ell_e)$ with $\|g_e-\phi_e\|_{L^2(e)}<\epsilon/\sqrt{|E|}$. The edge-product function $\phi=(\phi_e)$ has zero endpoint traces, hence belongs to $V_D$, and $\|g-\phi\|_H^2=\sum_e\|g_e-\phi_e\|_{L^2(e)}^2<\epsilon^2$. Thus the range of i is dense in H. [F2, F3, A2, given, choose, algebra]

## Statement

Use the data of [[def-finite-weighted-network-diffusion-data]] and write
$L=L_D$. For any $t\ge0$, the homogeneous exact semigroup
$$S_D(t)=e^{-tM^{-1}L}$$
maps entrywise nonnegative initial vectors to entrywise nonnegative vectors.
For a forward Euler step of size $\tau\ge0$, the map
$$E_F(\tau)=I-\tau M^{-1}L$$
is entrywise nonnegative, and hence positivity preserving for every
nonnegative input, exactly when
$$0\le\tau\le\tau_F:=\min_{\substack{i\in I\\L_{ii}>0}}\frac{m_i}{L_{ii}},$$
where the minimum of an empty set is $+\infty$. For every $\tau>0$, the
backward Euler map $(M+\tau L)^{-1}M$ exists and is positivity preserving.
The forward Euler threshold is sharp for positivity of the full step matrix.

2.1 The mass state $p=Mu$ satisfies $p'=Qp$ for the homogeneous network equation. Its solution is $p(t)=e^{tQ}p(0)$. Since $M$ and $M^{-1}$ are entrywise positive diagonal matrices, $$u(t)=M^{-1}e^{tQ}Mu(0)=e^{-tM^{-1}L}u(0),$$ where the second equality follows term by term from the matrix exponential series applied to the similarity $M^{-1}QM=-M^{-1}L$. Steps 1.1–1.2 therefore prove positivity of $S_D(t)$ for both boundary cases. [F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

## Definition

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty bounded connected polyhedral open set, and let $\mathcal T_h$ be a finite matching affine simplicial mesh of $\Omega$ as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. Fix a polynomial degree $k\ge1$. Let $V_h$ be the real scalar conforming polynomial space of [[def-broken-and-conforming-polynomial-spaces]], viewed as a subspace of $H^1(\Omega)$ by [[thm-matching-continuous-piecewise-polynomials-are-wkp]], and let $Y_h:=V_h\cap H^1_0(\Omega)$, where $H^1_0$ is the closure convention of [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]; [[lem-nitsche-h-one-zero-functions-have-zero-facet-traces]] proves its facet-trace consequence. Boundary facets form $\mathcal F_h^\partial$. If $F\in\mathcal F_h^\partial$, let $K_F$ be its unique incident cell, $n_F$ its outward unit normal, $|F|$ its $(d-1)$-dimensional measure, and set $h_F:=|K_F|/|F|>0$. For functions with a defined boundary normal trace write $\partial_n v:=\nabla v\cdot n_F$ on $F$.

Let $\mathcal X_h$ consist of $v\in H^1(\Omega)$ such that for every cell $K$ there is $s_K>1/2$ with $v|_K\in H^{1+s_K}(K)$. By [[lem-nitsche-fractional-face-trace-on-simplex]], $v$ has an $L^2(F)$ trace on each facet, and each component of $\nabla(v|_K)$ is in $H^{s_K}(K)$, hence has an $L^2(F)$ trace by the same lemma; the derivative mapping follows from $|\xi_j|\langle\xi\rangle^{s_K}\le\langle\xi\rangle^{1+s_K}$ in the Bessel-potential norm. Thus $\partial_n v$ and all displayed integrals are defined. In particular, $V_h\subseteq\mathcal X_h$ and the exact/adjoint functions in the later regularity hypotheses lie in $\mathcal X_h$. For a dimensionless penalty coefficient $\gamma_0\ge0$ and symmetry parameter $\theta\in\{0,1\}$, define the same bilinear formula on $\mathcal X_h\times\mathcal X_h$:
$$a_h^\theta(v,w):=\int_\Omega\nabla v\cdot\nabla w\,dx-\sum_{F\in\mathcal F_h^\partial}\int_F(\partial_n v)w\,dS-\theta\sum_{F\in\mathcal F_h^\partial}\int_Fv(\partial_n w)\,dS+\gamma_0\sum_{F\in\mathcal F_h^\partial}h_F^{-1}\int_Fvw\,dS.$$
For $f\in L^2(\Omega)$ and boundary data $g$ with the displayed integrals finite, define
$$\ell_h^\theta(w_h):=\int_\Omega f w_h\,dx-\theta\sum_{F\in\mathcal F_h^\partial}\int_Fg(\partial_n w_h)\,dS+\gamma_0\sum_{F\in\mathcal F_h^\partial}h_F^{-1}\int_Fg w_h\,dS.$$
The **nonsymmetric Nitsche form** is $a_h^0$; it has the consistency flux in the trial slot only. The **symmetric Nitsche form** is $a_h^1$; it has both transposed consistency fluxes. The discrete weak-boundary problem is the standard Nitsche method when $\gamma_0>0$: it seeks $u_h\in V_h$ such that $a_h^\theta(u_h,w_h)=\ell_h^\theta(w_h)$ for every $w_h\in V_h$. This extension makes expressions such as $a_h^\theta(u,w_h)$ and $a_h^\theta(e,\zeta-z_h)$ well-defined when the exact and adjoint functions have the stated cellwise regularity. The boundary penalty is $\gamma_0/h_F$; $h_F$ is the cell-face height divided by $d$, not the face diameter. The zero value $\gamma_0=0$ is used only for the penalty-free algebraic comparison.

The energy seminorm and the comparison seminorm used below are
$$\|v\|_{E,h}^2:=\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2+\sum_{F\in\mathcal F_h^\partial}h_F^{-1}\|v\|_{L^2(F)}^2,\qquad \|v\|_{\#,h}^2:=\|v\|_{E,h}^2+\sum_{F\in\mathcal F_h^\partial}h_F\|\partial_n v\|_{L^2(F)}^2.$$

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D$ have finite Lebesgue measure. For every product-measurable kernel $a\in L^2(D\times D;\mathbb C)$, the formula $T_av(x)=\int_Da(x,y)v(y)dy$ defines a representative-independent complex-linear map $L^2(D;\mathbb C)\to L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ and $\|T_a\|\le\|a\|_{L^2(D\times D)}$. Consequently, under [[def-volume-integral-scattering-model]] with $0<|D|<\infty$,
$$\|K_k\|_{L^2\to L^2}\le\|G_k(\cdot-\cdot)q(\cdot)\|_{L^2(D\times D)}\le\|q\|_\infty\sqrt{\frac{|D|\,\operatorname{diam}(D)}{4\pi}}.$$
For $|D|=0$ the operator is zero.

1.1 On the product space, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\int_{D\times D}|a(x,y)u(y)|dxdy\le\|a\|_2\bigl(|D|\int_D|u(y)|^2dy\bigr)^{1/2}<\infty$. Hence the section integral defining $T_au$ exists absolutely for almost every $x$ and is measurable by F3. [F1, F2, F3, given]

## Statement

Use the model of [[def-supg-general-convection-diffusion-reaction-model]] and form/parameter of [[def-supg-general-residual-form]]. Assume Countable Choice, and let $u\in C^2(\overline\Omega)$ solve the stated strong problem. For every continuous, zero-boundary function $w$ whose restriction to each cell has square-integrable values and square-integrable weak first derivatives, define
$$\|w\|_{\mathrm{SD},h}^2:=\epsilon\|\nabla w\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2+\omega\|w\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2+\sum_K\delta_K\|b\cdot\nabla w\|_{L^2(K)}^2.$$
$$M_2:=|\Omega|^{1/2}\|D^2u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},\quad B:=\|b\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},\quad C:=\|c\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},\quad \delta_*:=\max_K\delta_K.$$
Then the discrete form is coercive:
$$a_h(v_h,v_h)\ge\frac34\|v_h\|_{\mathrm{SD},h}^2\qquad(v_h\in V_h),$$
the discrete problem has a unique solution $u_h$, and the method is consistent, $a_h(u,v_h)=F_h(v_h)$. Moreover, with $C_*$ depending only on dimension, shape regularity, and the interpolation constant,
$$\|u-u_h\|_{\mathrm{SD},h}\le C_*M_2\left[\left(\sqrt{\epsilon}+\frac{B}{\sqrt{\omega}}\right)h+\left(\sqrt{\omega}+\frac{C}{\sqrt{\omega}}\right)h^2+B\sqrt{\delta_*}\,h+\sqrt{\delta_*}\left(\sqrt d\,\epsilon+Bh+Ch^2\right)\right].$$
This is a P1 estimate for the stated strong regularity and parameter branch; it does not claim stability for unrestricted multidimensional parameters or weaker regularity.

3.1 The linear map $V_h\to V_h^*$ induced by $a_h$ has zero kernel: if $a_h(w_h,v_h)=0$ for all $v_h$, test with $v_h=w_h$ and use step 2.1 to get $w_h=0$. ## Statement

For the ideal-gas model in [[def-compressible-navier-stokes-fourier-model]], the mathematical entropy $\eta=-\rho s$ has positive-definite Hessian on $\mathcal G$. Its entropy variables are

$$v(U)=\nabla_U\eta(U)=\left(c_v\gamma-s-\frac{\beta|u|^2}{2},\ \beta u,\ -\beta\right),\qquad \beta=\frac{c_v\rho}{\varepsilon}=\frac1T.$$

The Euler entropy flux $q_j(U)=\eta(U)u_j$ is compatible with $F_j$, meaning $\nabla_Uq_j=(\nabla_U\eta)^TDF_j$, and its entropy potential is $\psi_j(U)=v(U)^TF_j(U)-q_j(U)=\rho R u_j$. Consequently $U\mapsto v(U)$ is a local diffeomorphism at every $U\in\mathcal G$ and $\eta$ is strictly convex on $\mathcal G$.

1.1 Set $\varepsilon=E-|m|^2/(2\rho)$ and $u=m/\rho$. Rewriting the entropy gives $\eta=-c_v\rho\log((\gamma-1)\varepsilon)+c_v\gamma\rho\log\rho-s_0\rho$. For an increment $\delta U=(a,b,c)$, its first internal-energy variation is $\delta\varepsilon=c-u\cdot b+|u|^2a/2$, and its second directional variation is $D^2\varepsilon[\delta U,\delta U]=-|b-ua|^2/\rho$. The chain rule therefore yields $D^2\eta[\delta U,\delta U]=c_v\left(\frac{\gamma}{\rho}a^2-\frac{2}{\varepsilon}a\,\delta\varepsilon+\frac{\rho}{\varepsilon^2}(\delta\varepsilon)^2+\frac1{\varepsilon}|b-ua|^2\right)$. The first three terms have matrix $\begin{pmatrix}\gamma/\rho&-1/\varepsilon\\-1/\varepsilon&\rho/\varepsilon^2\end{pmatrix}$, whose leading diagonal entry is positive and determinant is $(\gamma-1)/\varepsilon^2>0$. The last term is nonnegative. If the full quadratic form is zero, then $a=\delta\varepsilon=0$ and $b=0$; the formula for $\delta\varepsilon$ then gives $c=0$. Thus the Hessian is positive definite. [F1, algebra]

## Example

Assume Countable Choice. Map $[-1,1]^2$ by the area-preserving shear $\Phi(x,y)=(x,y+x^2/4)$. Triangulate the square once along the southwest-to-northeast diagonal and once along the other diagonal; map both meshes by the same $\Phi$. Every source-target overlap has area $1$. If the source cell values are $2$ and $0$, each target average is $1$, source and target total mass are both $4$, and all target values remain nonnegative.

1.1 The shear is a global $C^1$ diffeomorphism with inverse $(X,Y)\mapsto(X,Y-X^2/4)$ and derivative $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\x/2&1\end{pmatrix}$ of determinant $1$. Apply [F4] to each overlap to see that its physical area equals the reference overlap area. In the reference square, the two diagonals meet at the center; the two diagonals divide the square into four corner triangles, each with base $2$ along a side and altitude $1$ to the center, so each nonempty source-target overlap has area $1$. [F1, F4, A1, given, algebra]

## Statement

For every $p\ge1$, the one-dimensional GLL rule integrates all polynomials of degree at most $2p-1$ exactly and has positive weights. If $f=\sum_{n=0}^pa_nP_n$, then
$$Q_p(f^2)-\int_{-1}^1f^2=\frac{2(p+1)}{p(2p+1)}a_p^2.$$
For every $v\in\mathbb Q_p([-1,1]^d)$,
$$\|v\|_{L^2}^2\le Q_p^{\otimes d}(v^2)\le3^d\|v\|_{L^2}^2,\qquad \|\nabla v\|_{L^2}^2\le Q_p^{\otimes d}(|\nabla v|^2)\le3^d\|\nabla v\|_{L^2}^2.$$
The same inequalities hold on affine boxes under the transported rule. If a scalar coefficient $a$ satisfies $0<\underline a\le a(x)\le\overline a$ throughout a box, the sampled form $Q_{K,p}(a|\nabla v|^2)$ is equivalent to the exact weighted energy $\int_Ka|\nabla v|^2$ with lower factor $\underline a/\overline a$ and upper factor $3^d\overline a/\underline a$. These are p-uniform stability bounds; they do not bound the Strang consistency defect or equate quadrature with exact Galerkin assembly.

1.1 Define $g(x)=(x^2-1)P_p'(x)$; it vanishes at all GLL nodes and has degree $p+1$. For $p\ge2$, divide any polynomial $f$ of degree at most $2p-1$ as $f=gr+s$ with $\deg r\le p-2$ and $\deg s\le p$. Integration by parts gives $\int_{-1}^1gr=-\int_{-1}^1P_p(2xr+(x^2-1)r')=0$, since the boundary term vanishes and the bracket has degree at most $p-1$. The quadrature of $gr$ is also zero because $g$ vanishes at every node, while the interpolatory definition integrates $s$ exactly. Thus $Q_p(f)=\int f$. For $p=1$, interpolatory exactness through degree $p=1$ is the required degree $2p-1=1$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

## Example

Use the period-$3$ one-dimensional grid with nodes $0,1,2$, $h=1$, and one time step $\Delta t=1$. Set
$$b(x)=\frac5{12}-\frac16\cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi x}{3}\right)-\frac1{2\sqrt3}\sin\!\left(\frac{2\pi x}{3}\right).$$
This is a smooth periodic velocity. Start with grid values $(U_0,U_1,U_2)=(0,0,1)$, which are samples of the smooth nonnegative period-$3$ function
$$u_0(x)=\frac{16}{9}\sin^2\!\left(\frac{\pi x}{3}\right)\sin^2\!\left(\frac{\pi(x-1)}{3}\right).$$

1.1 The squared-sine factors are smooth and period $3$; the value is zero at nodes $0$ and $1$ and equals $1$ at node $2$. Direct substitution into $b$ gives $(b(0),b(1),b(2))=(1/4,1/4,3/4)$. Therefore the three lifted feet are $-1/4,3/4,5/4$. Their interpolation rows, in node order $0,1,2$, are $(3/4,0,1/4)$, $(1/4,3/4,0)$, and $(0,3/4,1/4)$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $\Omega=\prod_{j=1}^d(0,\ell_j)$ be the bounded open fundamental box used for Lebesgue measure, and let $Q=\prod_{j=1}^d[0,\ell_j)$ be its half-open grid-indexing copy. Let $\Phi$ be the periodic $C^1$ characteristic diffeomorphism of [[lem-periodic-characteristic-map-is-orientation-preserving]], and let $A_i$ be a finite tensor-grid cell in $Q$ with nonempty interior. Then $D_i:=\Phi^{-1}(A_i)$, interpreted on the torus and represented in $\Omega$, is Lebesgue measurable and satisfies
$$0<|D_i|<\infty.$$
The finite family of departure cells is a partition whenever the arrival cells form a partition.

2.1 The interior of $A_i$ is nonempty, so its lift-preimage is a nonempty open periodic set. It contains an open product box. In each of its finitely many coordinate intervals, take a point away from the discrete period lattice; the resulting point is in the interior of one lattice tile. A sufficiently small ball around it lies both in that tile and in the lift-preimage. Translate the ball by a period vector into $\Omega$. By [F3] it has positive measure; [F5] then gives $|D_i|>0$. Also $D_i\subseteq\Omega$, and [F4] and [F5] give $|D_i|\le|\Omega|=\prod_j\ell_j<\infty$. [given, A1, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, choose, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $\Omega=\prod_{j=1}^d(0,\ell_j)$ be the bounded open fundamental box used for Lebesgue measure, and let $Q=\prod_{j=1}^d[0,\ell_j)$ be its half-open grid-indexing copy. Let $\Phi$ be the periodic $C^1$ characteristic diffeomorphism of [[lem-periodic-characteristic-map-is-orientation-preserving]], and let $A_i$ be a finite tensor-grid cell in $Q$ with nonempty interior. Then $D_i:=\Phi^{-1}(A_i)$, interpreted on the torus and represented in $\Omega$, is Lebesgue measurable and satisfies
$$0<|D_i|<\infty.$$
The finite family of departure cells is a partition whenever the arrival cells form a partition.

1.1 Write the grid cell as $A_i=\prod_j[a_j,b_j)$ in $Q$, and let $\Lambda=\prod_j\ell_j\mathbb Z$ be the period lattice. Its torus lift is the countable union $\widehat A_i=\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}\prod_j[a_j+k_j\ell_j,b_j+k_j\ell_j)$. Each half-open box is Borel, so $\widehat A_i$ is Borel; continuity of $\Phi$ makes $\Phi^{-1}(\widehat A_i)$ Borel, and its intersection with the open box $\Omega$ is Borel. By [A1] and [F2], this representative of $D_i$ is Lebesgue measurable. Equivariance under $\Lambda$ makes the torus preimage independent of the chosen lift. Since [F1] makes $\Phi$ a bijection on the torus, inverse images preserve disjointness and unions, so departure cells form a partition whenever the arrival cells do. [given, A1, F1, F2, algebra]

## Definition

Let $d,q\ge1$, $T>0$, and let $A$ be a nonempty compact subset of
$\mathbb R^q$ (a finite action set is included). For each $a\in A$, let
$b_a:\mathbb T^d\times[0,T]\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$\ell_a:\mathbb T^d\times[0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and jointly
continuous in $(x,t,a)$. Write $b_a,\ell_a$ also for their periodic lifts to
$\mathbb R^d\times[0,T]$. Assume there are constants $B,L<\infty$ such that
$$|b_a(x,t)|\le B,\qquad |\ell_a(x,t)|\le L,$$
and for all $a\in A$, $x,y\in\mathbb R^d$, and $t,s\in[0,T]$,
$$|b_a(x,t)-b_a(y,s)|+|\ell_a(x,t)-\ell_a(y,s)| \le L(|x-y|+|t-s|).$$
Given continuous periodic initial data $u_0:\mathbb T^d\to\mathbb R$, define
$$H(x,t,p)=\max_{a\in A}\{-b_a(x,t)\cdot p-\ell_a(x,t)\}.$$
The **periodic first-order controlled Hamilton–Jacobi Cauchy problem** is
$$u_t+H(x,t,Du)=0\quad\text{on }\mathbb T^d\times(0,T),\qquad u(x,0)=u_0(x).$$
The signs are fixed by
$u_t=\min_{a\in A}\{b_a\cdot Du+\ell_a\}$. A finite control
discretization $A_k\subset A$ is admissible when, for every $R<\infty$,
$$\eta_k(R):=\sup_{x,t,|p|\le R}|H_k(x,t,p)-H(x,t,p)|\longrightarrow0, \qquad H_k(x,t,p):=\max_{a\in A_k}(-b_a\cdot p-\ell_a).$$
Exact minimization over $A$ corresponds to $\eta_k=0$. Scheme convergence below
uses this explicit control-grid error whenever the controls are discretized.

## Definition

Let $d,q\ge1$, $T>0$, and let $A$ be a nonempty compact subset of
$\mathbb R^q$ (a finite action set is included). For each $a\in A$, let
$b_a:\mathbb T^d\times[0,T]\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$\ell_a:\mathbb T^d\times[0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and jointly
continuous in $(x,t,a)$. Write $b_a,\ell_a$ also for their periodic lifts to
$\mathbb R^d\times[0,T]$. Assume there are constants $B,L<\infty$ such that
$$|b_a(x,t)|\le B,\qquad |\ell_a(x,t)|\le L,$$
and for all $a\in A$, $x,y\in\mathbb R^d$, and $t,s\in[0,T]$,
$$|b_a(x,t)-b_a(y,s)|+|\ell_a(x,t)-\ell_a(y,s)| \le L(|x-y|+|t-s|).$$
Given continuous periodic initial data $u_0:\mathbb T^d\to\mathbb R$, define
$$H(x,t,p)=\max_{a\in A}\{-b_a(x,t)\cdot p-\ell_a(x,t)\}.$$
The **periodic first-order controlled Hamilton–Jacobi Cauchy problem** is
$$u_t+H(x,t,Du)=0\quad\text{on }\mathbb T^d\times(0,T),\qquad u(x,0)=u_0(x).$$
The signs are fixed by
$u_t=\min_{a\in A}\{b_a\cdot Du+\ell_a\}$. A finite control
discretization $A_k\subset A$ is admissible when, for every $R<\infty$,
$$\eta_k(R):=\sup_{x,t,|p|\le R}|H_k(x,t,p)-H(x,t,p)|\longrightarrow0, \qquad H_k(x,t,p):=\max_{a\in A_k}(-b_a\cdot p-\ell_a).$$
Exact minimization over $A$ corresponds to $\eta_k=0$. Scheme convergence below
uses this explicit control-grid error whenever the controls are discretized.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice for the finite-dimensional Gaussian probability law.
Let $k\ge1$ and let $p$ be a positive integer, with $p\ge2$ over $\mathbb R$
and $p\ge1$ over normalized $\mathbb C$. Let $G\in F^{k\times(k+p)}$ have iid entries as in
[[def-standard-real-and-normalized-complex-gaussian-matrix-law]]. Then $G$
has full row rank almost surely and
$$\mathbb E\|G^\dagger\|_F^2= \begin{cases}k/(p-1),&F=\mathbb R,\\k/p,&F=\mathbb C.\end{cases}$$
The complex entry convention is variance one, $\mathbb E|G_{ij}|^2=1$. Write
$G^\dagger=G^+$ for the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse of
[[def-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse]]. On the full-row-rank event,
$$G^\dagger=G^*(GG^*)^{-1},\qquad (G^\dagger)^*G^\dagger=(GG^*)^{-1}.$$
Here $U\sim\Gamma(a,\theta)$ means that $U$ has density
$u^{a-1}e^{-u/\theta}/(\theta^a\Gamma(a))$ for $u>0$. For every diagonal
index $i$, $((GG^*)^{-1})_{ii}$ has distribution $1/U$ with
$U\sim\Gamma((p+1)/2,2)$ over $\mathbb R$ and $U\sim\Gamma(p+1,1)$ over
$\mathbb C$.

2.1 For each fixed $H$, choose orthonormal coordinates in which $P$ is diagonal with $p+1$ ones. Independence of $g$ from $H$ and invariance [F7] show that $gPg^*$ is a sum of $p+1$ independent squared real Gaussians, or squared moduli of normalized complex Gaussians. Apply [F10] separately on the open half-lines via $x=\sqrt u$ and $x=-\sqrt u$ (absolute derivative $1/(2\sqrt u)$); the omitted point has zero measure. Adding the two densities gives the real square density $u^{-1/2}e^{-u/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}=u^{-1/2}e^{-u/2}/(\sqrt2\Gamma(1/2))$ by [F6]. For the complex square law, [F11] applied to the normalized density gives $1=\pi^{-1}\sigma(S^1)\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2}r\,dr=\sigma(S^1)/(2\pi)$, so $\sigma(S^1)=2\pi$. Applying the same formula with any nonnegative Borel function of $r^2$, and then [F10] with $u=r^2$, shows that the squared modulus has density $e^{-u}$ on $(0,\infty)$. The first real square is thus Gamma$(1/2,2)$ and the complex square Gamma$(1,1)$, the latter normalized by [F12]. If independent Gamma variables have common scale $\theta$ and shapes $a,b$, [F5] and the diffeomorphism $(u,v)\mapsto(u,s=u+v)$ of the positive quadrant onto $0<u<s$, of determinant one in [F10], show that their sum has convolution density with normalization $1/(\theta^{a+b}\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b))$ and numerator $e^{-s/\theta}\int_0^s u^{a-1}(s-u)^{b-1}du$. For each $s>0$, substituting $u=st$ by [F10] and using [F3] makes this $e^{-s/\theta}s^{a+b-1}B(a,b)$, which is the Gamma density of shape $a+b$ and scale $\theta$. Iterating this finite convolution gives $gPg^*\sim\Gamma((p+1)/2,2)$ over $\mathbb R$ and $gPg^*\sim\Gamma(p+1,1)$ over $\mathbb C$. Tonelli [F5] integrates first over $g$ and then over $H$, so the reciprocal law holds unconditionally for the first diagonal entry; row permutation invariance gives the same law for every index. [step 1.1, F1, F3, F5, F6, F7, F10, F11, F12, choose]

## Statement

Use the data and aliases of
[[lem-ewald-pme-spline-alias-and-dft-normalization]]. Write
$h_r(0)=1$ and, for $u_r=k_r/M_r\ne0$,
$h_r(n)=|u_r/(u_r+n)|^P$ for $n\ne0$; when $u_r=0$, set $h_r(n)=0$ for
$n\ne0$. Put
$$a_r=\sum_{n\ne0}h_r(n).$$
For $P\ge3$, define
$$v_r=\sum_{n\ne0}|k_r+nM_r|h_r(n),\qquad J_{k,r}=(|k_r|+v_r)\prod_{s\ne r}(1+a_s)-|k_r|,$$
and
$$B_k=2\pi\|A^{-T}\|_2\left(\sum_{r=1}^3J_{k,r}^2\right)^{1/2}.$$
For $P\ge3$ the physical derivative alias error satisfies
$$\|\nabla_xb_k(t)-\nabla_xa_k(t)\|_2\le B_k.$$
Each series has a finite p-series controller: for $0<|u_r|<1/2$,
$$a_r\le2\frac{|u_r|^P}{(1-|u_r|)^P}\zeta(P),\qquad v_r\le2M_r\frac{|u_r|^P}{(1-|u_r|)^{P-1}}\zeta(P-1),$$
where $\zeta(s)=\sum_{m\ge1}m^{-s}$ for $s>1$. After summing exactly over
$1\le|n|\le J_0$, the respective omitted tails are at most
$$2\frac{|u_r|^P}{(1-|u_r|)^P}\frac{J_0^{1-P}}{P-1},\qquad 2M_r\frac{|u_r|^P}{(1-|u_r|)^{P-1}}\frac{J_0^{2-P}}{P-2}.$$

For the approved $P=2$ case, the absolute derivative p-series above diverges
when $u_r\ne0$. Instead use the finite derivative of the local piecewise
window sum. At every open mesh box and each one-sided knot limit, put
$$C_{k,r}=\frac{2M_r}{|D(k)|}+2\pi|k_r|,\qquad B_k=\|A^{-T}\|_2\left(\sum_{r=1}^3C_{k,r}^2\right)^{1/2}.$$
This is a computable finite bound for the same physical derivative error. At a
grid knot, use the declared $\mathfrak d_k(t)$ branch from
[[def-ewald-pme-cardinal-assignment-model]]: it is a selected one-sided value
or their average and obeys the bound, but is not asserted to be a classical
derivative there. Thus for the full $P\ge2$ range the bound is on
$\mathfrak d_k(t)-\nabla_xa_k(t)$, with $\mathfrak d_k=\nabla_xb_k$ wherever
the classical derivative exists.

1.2 Now let $P=2$. The convolution $W_2(u)=\int_0^1\mathbf1_{[0,1]}(u-s)ds$ is the length of $[0,1]\cap[u-1,u]$, hence is $u$ on $[0,1]$, $2-u$ on $[1,2]$, and $0$ outside $[0,2]$. Its derivative is $1$ on $(0,1)$, $-1$ on $(1,2)$, and $0$ outside, with the indicated one-sided values at $0,1,2$. On every open mesh box, only finitely many window translates are nonzero, so direct differentiation gives $\partial_{t_r}b_k(t)=\frac{M_r}{\overline{D(k)}}\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb Z^3} W_2'(M_rt_r-\ell_r)\prod_{s\ne r}W_2(M_st_s-\ell_s) e^{-2\pi i\sum_sk_s\ell_s/M_s}.$ The periodic residue version is identical because $k_s$ are integers and the phase is unchanged when $\ell_s$ is shifted by $M_s$. For every non-knot $y$, one translate lies in $(0,1)$ and one in $(1,2)$, so $\sum_{\ell_r}|W_2'(y-\ell_r)|=2$; at a knot the same sum of absolute one-sided values is at most $2$. Also $W_2\ge0$ and $\sum_\ell W_2(y-\ell)=1$ by the partition identity proved in [F1]. Therefore $|\partial_{t_r}b_k|\le2M_r/|D(k)|$. Since $|\partial_{t_r}a_k|=2\pi|k_r|$, the fractional derivative error is at most $C_{k,r}$. [F1, F2, algebra]

$$a_r=\sum_{n\ne0}h_r(n).$$

$$v_r=\sum_{n\ne0}|k_r+nM_r|h_r(n),\qquad J_{k,r}=(|k_r|+v_r)\prod_{s\ne r}(1+a_s)-|k_r|,$$

$$B_k=2\pi\|A^{-T}\|_2\left(\sum_{r=1}^3J_{k,r}^2\right)^{1/2}.$$

$$\|\nabla_xb_k(t)-\nabla_xa_k(t)\|_2\le B_k.$$
Each series has a finite p-series controller: for $0<|u_r|<1/2$,
$$a_r\le2\frac{|u_r|^P}{(1-|u_r|)^P}\zeta(P),\qquad v_r\le2M_r\frac{|u_r|^P}{(1-|u_r|)^{P-1}}\zeta(P-1),$$

$$2\frac{|u_r|^P}{(1-|u_r|)^P}\frac{J_0^{1-P}}{P-1},\qquad 2M_r\frac{|u_r|^P}{(1-|u_r|)^{P-1}}\frac{J_0^{2-P}}{P-2}.$$

window sum. At every open mesh box and each one-sided knot limit, put
$$C_{k,r}=\frac{2M_r}{|D(k)|}+2\pi|k_r|,\qquad B_k=\|A^{-T}\|_2\left(\sum_{r=1}^3C_{k,r}^2\right)^{1/2}.$$

## Statement

Let $ABCD$ be a strictly convex planar quadrilateral in counterclockwise boundary order. Lift its four sites using the common formal heights of [[def-lexicographic-lift-tie-break]]. Let $g_{AC}$ and $g_{BD}$ be the piecewise-affine interpolants on the two diagonal triangulations. Define each interpolant's integral over the quadrilateral as the sum over its two triangles of triangle area times the average of the three vertex heights. If the lifted point $D$ lies strictly below the affine plane through the lifts of $A,B,C$ (the illegal-incircle sign by the coefficientwise determinant identity), then
$$\int_{ABCD}g_{BD}<\int_{ABCD}g_{AC}$$
in the lexicographic order of the formal lift field.

1.1 The two interpolants agree at the four boundary vertices. Their common diagonal intersection $O$ lies strictly inside both diagonals. On the four triangles formed by $O$ and the four boundary edges, each interpolant is affine; their difference is zero at the two boundary endpoints and equals $\delta:=g_{BD}(O)-g_{AC}(O)$ at $O$. [given, F1, A1, construct]

4.1 The row-subtraction and height-column elimination used in [F2] are polynomial determinant identities in the site heights, so they remain valid coefficientwise after each height is replaced by its formal perturbation. By [F3]–[F4], one common formal configuration resolves a zero constant term. Thus the below-plane condition is exactly the illegal incircle sign and its flip strictly decreases the potential. ## Statement

Let $d\in\{2,3\}$ and let $P$ be a finite indexed weighted site set of affine dimension $d$ in $\mathbb R^d$. Lift each site to height $h_i=\|p_i\|^2-w_i+\varepsilon^{2^{r_i}}$ in the fixed ordered formal field of [[def-lexicographic-lift-tie-break]]. A **lower simplex** is the projection of $d+1$ affinely independent lifted sites whose graph hyperplane has every lifted site on or above it. Then the lower simplices cover $\operatorname{conv}(P)$ and intersect in common faces. Each lower simplex has a weakly empty power sphere for the original unperturbed weighted sites.

1.1 Fix $x\in\operatorname{conv}(P)$. A feasible representation is a vector $(\lambda_i)_{i\in P}$ with $\lambda_i\ge0$, $\sum_i\lambda_i=1$, and $\sum_i\lambda_i p_i=x$. Its formal height is $H(\lambda)=\sum_i\lambda_i h_i$. If its support has more than $d+1$ sites, the vectors $(p_i,1)\in\mathbb R^{d+1}$ are linearly dependent, so there is a nonzero vector $(\alpha_i)$ on that support with $\sum_i\alpha_i=0$ and $\sum_i\alpha_i p_i=0$. Such a vector has both positive and negative entries. Choose one of the two directions $\lambda+t\alpha$ that does not increase $H$ and increase $|t|$ until a coefficient first becomes zero. This preserves feasibility and reduces support. Repeating finitely gives a feasible representation of support at most $d+1$ with no greater height. [given, F1, algebra, algebra]

## Statement

Let $Q\in\mathbb K^{n\times d}$, $d\ge1$, have orthonormal columns,
and let $\ell_i=\|e_i^*Q\|_2^2$. Let $\pi$ be a probability vector
with $\pi_i\ge\beta\ell_i/d$ for $0<\beta\le1$, and draw $S$ by
[[alg-leverage-score-row-sampling-sketch]] with replacement. For
$0<\varepsilon,\delta<1$, if
$$
m\ge\frac{8d}{\beta\varepsilon^2}\log\left(\frac{2d}{\delta}\right),
$$
then with probability at least $1-\delta$,
$$
\|Q^*S^*SQ-I_d\|_2\le\varepsilon.
$$
Equivalently, $S$ is an $\varepsilon$-subspace embedding for
$\operatorname{Ran}(Q)$. In the usual confidence range
$0<\delta\le1/2$, the simpler sufficient condition
$$
m\ge\frac{16d}{\beta\varepsilon^2}\log\left(\frac d\delta\right)
$$
follows. For a matrix $A$ of rank $d$, any orthonormal basis $Q$ of
$\operatorname{Ran}(A)$ gives the corresponding embedding guarantee on
$\operatorname{Ran}(A)$.

1.1 Write $z_i=Q^*e_i\in\mathbb K^d$, so $\|z_i\|_2^2=\ell_i$. For draw $j$, let $J_j$ be its sampled index and define $Y_j=z_{J_j}z_{J_j}^*/\pi_{J_j}$. By [F2], the $Y_j$ are independent and $\mathbb E Y_j=\sum_{i:\pi_i>0}z_i z_i^*=Q^*Q=I_d$; terms with $\pi_i=0$ have $z_i=0$ by [F1] and contribute zero. [F1, F2, algebra]

## Statement

Let $\widehat X=\widehat X^*$ be a CARE candidate, $\widehat A_c=A-G\widehat X$, and
$$\mathcal L(E)=\widehat A_c^*E+E\widehat A_c,\qquad F_c(X)=A^*X+XA-XGX+Q.$$
Assume $\widehat A_c$ is certified Hurwitz, $\mathcal L$ is invertible on Hermitian matrices, and outward-verified bounds satisfy
$$\kappa\ge\|\mathcal L^{-1}\|_{F\to F},\quad r\ge\|F_c(\widehat X)\|_F,\quad g\ge\|G\|_2,$$
with $\rho>0$ such that
$$\kappa(r+g\rho^2)\le\rho,\qquad 2\kappa g\rho<1.$$
Then there is exactly one Hermitian CARE root in the closed Frobenius ball $\|X-\widehat X\|_F\le\rho$.

If also a verified Hermitian $W\succ0$ and $\gamma>0$ satisfy
$$-(\widehat A_c^*W+W\widehat A_c)\succeq\gamma I,\qquad 2\|W\|_2g\rho<\gamma,$$
then that root is Hurwitz-stabilizing. Under the standard CARE hypotheses of [[thm-care-stabilizing-psd-solution-and-value]], it is the unique stabilizing positive-semidefinite solution.

2.1 By [F5], $\|EGE\|_F\le g\|E\|_F^2$. The assumptions give $\|\mathcal T(E)\|_F\le\kappa(r+g\rho^2)\le\rho$ on the closed ball. Also $EGE-FGF=(E-F)GE+FG(E-F),$ so [F5] gives $\|\mathcal T(E)-\mathcal T(F)\|_F\le2\kappa g\rho\|E-F\|_F$ there. The Hermitian matrices form a closed finite-dimensional normed space, complete by [F9]. Iterating $\mathcal T$ from zero gives successive differences bounded by a geometric sequence of ratio $2\kappa g\rho<1$, hence a Cauchy sequence. ## Example

Take the single parallelogram cell with vertices $(0,0),(2,0),(3,1),(1,1)$, tensor $A=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)$, and affine state $u(x,y)=x+2y$. Prescribe on each boundary face its exact face mean. The cell center is $(3/2,1/2)$ and the face centers, in bottom/right/top/left order, are $(1,0),(5/2,1/2),(2,1),(1/2,1/2)$. This cell is skew: its right and left face normals are not parallel to the vectors from the cell center to those face centers.

2.1 The cell and face means of $u$ are $u_K=5/2$ and $(u_F)=(1,7/2,4,3/2)$. Substitution into [F1] gives $\sum_F|F|u_Fn_{K,F}=(2,4)$ and hence $G_Ku=(1,2)=\nabla u$. Each residual is zero: for example, on the bottom face $u_F-u_K=-3/2=G_Ku\cdot((-1/2,-1/2))$, and the same dot-product identity holds for the other three face centers. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

## Statement

For the data of [[def-overlapping-schwarz-subspace-correction-data]], every
local matrix $A_i=R_i^{\mathsf T}AR_i$ with $i\in\mathcal I$ is symmetric
positive definite and therefore invertible. If the coarse index $0$ is
present, then $A_0=P^{\mathsf T}AP$ is the SPD Galerkin coarse matrix. Hence
every exact local solve in the definition exists uniquely.

1.1 Fix any $i\in\mathcal I$ with $i\ne0$ and any nonzero $z\in\mathbb R^{n_i}$. Full column rank in [F1] gives $R_i z\ne0$, so $z^{\mathsf T}A_i z=(R_i z)^{\mathsf T}A(R_i z)>0.$ Also [F4] gives $A_i^{\mathsf T}=R_i^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}R_i=A_i$. Thus every such $A_i$ is SPD. [F1, F4, given, algebra]

## Definition

Use the exterior energy space $E^+(\Omega^+)$ and weak conormal conventions of [[def-bem-laplace-layer-potentials-and-energy-spaces]]. For $\phi\in H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ let
$$\mathcal A_\phi=\{(u^-,u^+)\in H^1(\Omega^-)\times E^+(\Omega^+):\gamma^-u^- -\gamma^+u^+=-\phi\}.$$
When it exists uniquely, denote by $D\phi$ the pair in $\mathcal A_\phi$ minimizing
$$\mathcal E(u^-,u^+)=\int_{\Omega^-}|\nabla u^-|^2dx+\int_{\Omega^+}|\nabla u^+|^2dx.$$
Existence, uniqueness, harmonicity, and equality of the weak conormals are proved in [[thm-bem-double-layer-transmission-jumps-and-bounds]].

For $\phi\in H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ and $x\notin\Gamma$, the corresponding classical potential, whose agreement with the minimizer is proved in [[thm-bem-double-layer-transmission-jumps-and-bounds]], is $D\phi(x)=\int_\Gamma\partial_{n_y}G_3(x,y)\phi(y)\,dS_y$. The sign in the imposed jump, $\gamma^-D\phi-\gamma^+D\phi=-\phi$, is the convention for this kernel.

## Definition

Let $e_1,\ldots,e_d$ be the standard basis of $\mathbb R^d$. By [[lem-periodic-cell-corrector-wellposedness]], let $\chi_j:=\chi_{e_j}$ be the unique mean-zero solution of the periodic cell equation. For $p=(p_1,\ldots,p_d)$ define $\chi_p=\sum_jp_j\chi_j$ and define the constant matrix $A^*$ by its columns:
$$A^*e_j:=\int_Ya(y)(e_j+\nabla\chi_j(y))\,dy.$$
Equivalently, $A^*p=\int_Ya(y)(p+\nabla\chi_p(y))dy$. All integrals are finite because $a\in L^\infty(Y)$ and $\nabla\chi_j\in L^2(Y)$. This definition does not itself assert symmetry or ellipticity.

## Statement

Let $\Omega=(0,L)$ and let $V_h$ be the conforming interval space in [[def-phase-field-discrete-realizations]], with center spacing $h$. Let $I_hv$ interpolate the absolutely-continuous representative of $v\in H^1(0,L)$ at the centers and extend it constantly to the two boundary half-cells. Let $P_h$ be the exact $L^2$-orthogonal projection onto $V_h$. There is a constant $C$ independent of $h$ such that
$$\|I_hv\|_{H^1}\le C\|v\|_{H^1},\qquad \|v-I_hv\|_{L^2}\le Ch\|v'\|_{L^2},\qquad \|P_hv\|_{H^1}\le C\|v\|_{H^1}.$$
In addition, $\|P_hv-v\|_{L^2}\le Ch\|v'\|_{L^2}$ for every $v\in H^1(0,L)$, $P_hv\to v$ in $H^1(0,L)$ for every $v\in H^1(0,L)$, and $P_hg\to g$ in $L^2(0,L)$ for every $g\in L^2(0,L)$ as $h\to0$.

3.1 If $v\in C^2([0,L])$, linear interpolation on each interior segment has $H^1$ error tending to zero, while on a boundary half-cell the derivative error is bounded by $\sqrt h\|v'\|_\infty$. Thus $\|I_hv-v\|_{H^1}\to0$. Step 2.1 applied to $v-I_hv$ gives $\|P_hv-I_hv\|_{H^1}\le C\|v-I_hv\|_{H^1}\to0$, so $P_hv\to v$ in $H^1$. [step 2.1, given, algebra]

## Statement

Use either connected no-flux realization in [[def-phase-field-discrete-realizations]]. In its finite-volume branch, assume the interior cell graph is connected; in its interval conforming branch, assume $N\ge1$. Write $\bar u_h=\langle u_h,\mathbf1\rangle_h/\langle\mathbf1,\mathbf1\rangle_h$ and $X_{h,0}=\{u_h:\bar u_h=0\}$. Then $A_h$ is self-adjoint and nonnegative, $\ker A_h=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf1\}$, and $\operatorname{ran}A_h=X_{h,0}$. The restriction $A_h:X_{h,0}\to X_{h,0}$ is positive definite and invertible. Define $A_h^\dagger u_h$ by first projecting $u_h$ onto $X_{h,0}$ and then applying this self-adjoint positive inverse. For each fixed finite mesh there is $C_h<\infty$ such that
$$\|u_h-\bar u_h\mathbf1\|_h^2\le C_h\langle A_hu_h,u_h\rangle_h.$$
For a one-cell mesh, $X_{h,0}=\{0\}$ and the inequality is vacuous.

1.1 The displayed bilinear form in [F1] is symmetric, so $A_h$ is self-adjoint. Its quadratic form is a sum of positive transmissibility-weighted squared jumps in the cell branch and is $\int_0^L|u_h'|^2$ in the interval branch, so it is nonnegative. If it is zero, every interior jump vanishes in the cell branch, and connectedness makes all cell values equal; in the interval branch the derivative is zero on every segment, and continuity makes the function constant. Conversely, constants have zero quadratic form. Thus $\ker A_h=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf1\}$. [F1, given, algebra]

For every $s>d/2$, every Schwartz function $f$ belongs to $H^s(\mathbb R^d)$, and the inverse Fourier transforms of $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ are Schwartz functions and are dense in $H^s(\mathbb R^d)$ of [[def-bessel-potential-space-and-restriction-quotient]]. The Fourier transform uses the negative-sign $2\pi$ convention.

1.2 Let $f$ be any Schwartz function and define $\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}dx$. Polynomial multiples of derivatives of $f$ have arbitrarily rapid decay by [F5], so they and their derivatives are integrable, including on each coordinate line with the other coordinates fixed. Differentiation in $\xi$ is justified by dominated convergence [F6] using these integrable moments. Apply [F7] on each coordinate line to such a function and its Fourier exponential: the derivative products are integrable and the boundary product tends to zero. Absolute Fubini [F6] then combines the coordinate identities and shows that every $\xi^\gamma D_\xi^\alpha\widehat f(\xi)$ is a finite linear combination of Fourier transforms of derivatives of polynomial multiples of $f$. Each such function is in $L^1$ by [F5], so its Fourier transform is bounded; hence $\widehat f$ is Schwartz and in $L^1$. In particular $\int(1+|\xi|^2)^s|\widehat f(\xi)|^2d\xi<\infty$, by polar integration [F6]. [F5, F6, F7, algebra]
